OVERVIEW

[
1
]

This matter raises issues regarding the last
Will and Testament of the Late Richard Winston Moore (
“Mr. Moore”
),
who passed away on December 19, 2015.

[
2
]

The dispute opposes principally the deceased’s
children, the plaintiff Ms. Lianne J. Moore (
“Lianne”
) and her brother,
the defendant Mr. John R. Moore (
“John”
), who are the residuary beneficiaries
of the remaining assets of the deceased’s Estate (the “
Trust Property
”).

[
3
]

Lianne is asking the Court to declare that her
father’s last Will and Testament,        (the
“Will”
)
[1]
is invalid. She invokes that
her father did not have the required capacity at the time of signing the Will and
that, in addition, his last wishes were impinged as a result of undue influence
exerted by her brother John.

[
4
]

For the reasons which follow, the Court finds
that the Will was signed while the testator’s mental condition had declined and
in circumstances where he could not reasonably understand and appreciate the
consequences and effects of the Will on his daughter.

[
5
]

He therefore lacked the required capacity to
sign critical provisions of the Will.

[
6
]

The Court concludes that the Will should be
declared null, except for specific bequests which the deceased had long before
manifested the intent of leaving to family members and close employees.

CONTEXT

[
7
]

Mr. Moore was a famous and iconic hockey player
of the Montreal Canadiens Hockey Team. He also established himself as a
successful and prosperous businessman, having founded and administered various
corporate entities
[2]

(the “
Moore Companies
”), which principally operated a rental business of
construction equipment (“
Moore Equipment
”).

[
8
]

The capital of the Trust Property consists
mostly of Mr. Moore’s wholly owned shares in the Moore Companies, as well as residential
real estate.

[
9
]

John and Lianne both worked with their father in
Moore Equipment. In essence, Lianne acted as her father’s assistant and John
was involved in the operations of the business.

[
10
]

Mr. Moore executed the Will concerned by the
present matter before a notary on February 12, 2014.

[
11
]

He designated three liquidators and trustees,
namely his son John, as well as the defendants Vincent Fazzolari (
“Vincent”
)
and Mtre Lionel Liber (
“Mtre Liber”
).

[
12
]

Vincent was the controller of the business and
was also a friend of Mr. Moore.

[
13
]

Mtre Liber is a lawyer who acts as a legal
advisor for the business’s litigation matters. He was consulted for certain of
Mr. Moore’s personal matters.

[
14
]

The present litigation solely concerns issues
raised regarding the Will.

[
15
]

Apart from her present demand to declare the
Will to be invalid, Lianne is also exercising legal remedies invoking her
rights as director or beneficiary of shares of the Moore Companies and of other
entities
mis en cause
. Those issues were split by judgment and are still
pending.
[3]

[
16
]

Mr. Moore was very close to Lianne and supported
her financially.

[
17
]

As for his relationship with John, it remained
more distant until 2013. John had prior to then principally been working away
in the Ontario business
[4]

since 1996. John joined the workforce of the Montreal office in 2013 and father
and son worked more closely together from then on.

[
18
]

Mr. Moore’s wishes have always been to treat his
children equally upon his death. He had a brief manuscript Will signed before
witnesses in 1977, which stipulates an equal treatment for both.
[5]
Although he was encouraged by
people in his environment to plan his succession, he was reluctant to sign a
new will, which he kept postponing.

[
19
]

The Will was signed on an urgent basis in
February 2014, under particular circumstances which constitute an essential
aspect of the Court’s analysis. They are described at length further below. Mr.
Moore was then 83 years of age. His medical records showed that his memory was
impaired and that he suffered from a mild cognitive impairment. His children and
close employees had noted a certain decrease in his mental functioning.

[
20
]

The Will stipulates conditions that are
detrimental to Lianne. In essence, her share of the Trust Property
[6]
is not paid directly to her, contrary
to John, but by the intermediary of a trust (the “
Lianne Trust”
) providing
for periodic payments which are far below the amounts from which Lianne benefitted
while her father was living. The capital of her share of the Trust Property is
kept in the Lianne Trust and can only be encroached upon certain conditions at
the trustees’ discretion. John is one of the trustees responsible for such
encroachment. At the end of Lianne’s life, what remains of the capital of the
Lianne Trust is awarded to John’s children.

[
21
]

The Will also provides that John will manage the
Moore Companies. No condition is stipulated to ensure Lianne’s employment.

ANALYSIS

1.

Mr. Moore’s testamentary incapacity

1.1

Legal
Principles

[
22
]

Articles 703 and 707 C.C.Q. enunciate the legal
rules applying to testamentary capacity. They provide as follows:

Art. 703. Every person having the
required capacity may, by will, provide otherwise than as by law for the
devolution upon his death of the whole or part of his property.

(…)

Art. 707. The capacity of the
testator is considered relatively to the time he made his will.

[
23
]

The Court of Appeal explains in
Brusenbauch

c.
Young
[7]

that the burden to demonstrate that the testator did not have the required
capacity at the time the will was executed rests upon the party who seeks the
nullity, given that one is presumed to be fully able to exercise his civil
rights:

[28]

I share this point of view. In
other words, referring to “
prima facie
” evidence is simply a
manner
of speaking
and does not detract from the fundamental rule of evidence
in civil matters, as expressed in articles 2803, para. 1, and 2804
C.C.Q.

Considering
the legal presumption of capacity established in matters of wills (in most
matters, indeed
, since
“
la capacité se présume
”), pursuant to article 4
C.C.Q.
,
the party who seeks the nullity of a will bears the onus of establishing, on a
balance of probabilities (“
par preuve prépondérante
”), the incapacity of
the testator at the time the will was signed.

Again, as is the case for undue influence (“
captation
”), this burden may
be discharged by direct or circumstantial evidence (i.e. presumptions of fact).

[29]

It goes without saying that if
the opposing party does not lead any contrary evidence, a court will most
likely conclude in favour of the party bearing the burden of proof. Of course,
this will not always be the case, if the evidence adduced by the plaintiff is
not sufficiently compelling, even in the absence of any contrary evidence. If
the plaintiff’s evidence is sufficient (art. 2804
C.C.Q.
), the
burden then switches to the defendant to establish, also on a balance of
probabilities, that, although the testator was generally incapable during the
period the will was signed, it was nevertheless signed during a lucid interval.

[30]

Finally, in most situations, it
is not without having first heard and canvassed all of the evidence offered by
all parties that a trial judge will be able to answer the question of whether
the party alleging the testator’s incapacity has discharged its burden.

(Reference omitted; emphasis added)

[
24
]

As the Court of Appeal specifies in
Pagé

c.
Henley
,
[8]

this burden of proof may be discharged by the demonstration that the testator’s
mental faculties did not permit him to understand and reasonably appreciate the
consequences of the provisions of his will:

[59]  De plus,
celui qui, comme l’appelante en l’espèce, prétend que le testateur n’était pas
apte à tester n’a pas à prouver que ce dernier souffrait d’aliénation mentale;
il
lui suffit d’établir qu’il ne jouissait pas suffisamment de ses facultés
intellectuelles pour comprendre et apprécier raisonnablement la
portée de ses dispositions testamentaires.

(References omitted; emphasis added)

[
25
]

Particular circumstances surrounding the signing
of the will may contribute to discharge this burden of proof, as the Supreme Court
concluded in
Guérin
v.
Guérin
:
[9]

The medical evidence in the case at bar, taken by itself was not
perhaps sufficient to establish a
prima facie
case of
testamentary incapacity. That evidence, however, must be considered in
conjunction with the surrounding circumstances. These included such matters as
(
1) the unseemly haste in the preparation and execution of the will; (2) the
fact that no attempt was made to obtain independent advice from the deceased's
own notary, who had acted for him for many years, and before whom he had
recently executed a will in authentic form; and (3) the absence of any
satisfactory explanation as to why the deceased should suddenly have decided to
bequeath all his property to one sister—with whom he had recently come to
reside—and to disinherit his brother and the other immediate relatives
benefited under the notarial will.

The Court below found that the medical evidence as to the physical
and mental condition of the deceased at the time the will was executed and the
circumstances surrounding its preparation and execution, were sufficient to
raise a
prima facie
presumption of incapacity that the burden
of establishing capacity to have made the will was therefore shifted to
appellants,
Russell v. Lefrançois,
and that they had failed to
discharge that burden. In my opinion, those findings should not be disturbed.

(References omitted; emphasis added)

[
26
]

The Supreme Court underlines that the conclusion
as to testamentary incapacity remains,
even accepting that the deceased knew and
approved of the contents of the will as it was put to him immediately before
execution.
[10]

[
27
]

Criteria have been elaborated by the doctrine
and the jurisprudence to assess whether a person has testamentary capacity. In
essence, the testator must enjoy his intellectual faculties to the point of
being able of understanding the meaning and of measuring
the scope of his testamentary dispositions. Again in
Pagé

c.
Henley,
the Court of Appeal discusses those criteria as follows:
[11]

[
66]

Après avoir exposé les caractéristiques cliniques correspondant à un
stade 6/7 de cette échelle de Reisberg, l’expert-neurologue
énumère les principaux critères à considérer pour évaluer le degré d’aptitude à
faire un testament ou un autre acte juridique ainsi que les critères cliniques
génériques pour déterminer la capacité d’une personne :

On
sait par ailleurs que les facultés intellectuelles et cognitives sont
nécessaires pour conclure à un acte légal tel un testament ou un mandat. La compréhension,
le jugement, l’autocritique et la mémoire sont des habiletés intellectuelles
essentielles pour une telle action.

Un
individu qui effectue un acte légal doit :

- Connaître
sans qu’on l’aide la nature et l’étendue des biens qu’il possède;

- Connaître
et comprendre la nature de l’acte qu’il s’apprête à effectuer;

- Connaître
(et se souvenir) le nom et l’identité des personnes destinataires;

- Connaître
la nature de la relation qu’il a avec eux;

- Comprendre
et se souvenir de tous ces faits;

- Être
capable de comprendre les relations de tous ces facteurs
entre eux;

- Avoir
la capacité de se souvenir de la décision qu’il a prise.

De même,
les critères cliniques génériques pour déterminer la capacité d’une personne
sont :

- La
capacité de communiquer sur le contenu de la décision à
prendre;

- Une
indication claire et répétée de préférence quant à la décision à
prendre;

- La
capacité de comprendre et de peser les options quant au
choix à prendre;

- La
capacité de rationaliser ce choix.

Un
syndrome démentiel, une maladie d’Alzheimer, peut donc affecter les capacités
intellectuelles essentielles à l’aptitude, influencer les éléments cliniques
génériques pour déterminer la capacité d’une personne et ainsi, rendre un
individu inapte et donc le placer dans un état d’incapacité à effectuer des
actes légaux.

[
67]

Ces critères identifiés par l’expert correspondent à ce que la
doctrine et la jurisprudence considèrent comme les éléments requis pour que le
testateur puisse avoir la volonté de tester. Ces éléments sont bien
exprimés par la professeure Morin :

26.

Pour être « capable de tester », le
testateur doit non seulement être juridiquement apte, mais il doit avoir la
« volonté de tester », ce qui signifie qu’il doit être en
mesure de donner un consentement. À ce sujet, la jurisprudence et la
doctrine s’accordent généralement pour affirmer qu’il faut que « le
testateur jouisse de ses facultés intellectuelles au
point de pouvoir envisager les divers éléments qui doivent déterminer
une personne à disposer de ses biens d’une manière plutôt que d’une
autre; de comprendre le sens et de mesurer la
portée de la disposition qu’elle va faire, et de s’y
arrêter volontairement »

(References omitted; emphasis added)

[
28
]

In
Phillips
c.
Douek
,
[12]
Justice Bachand, sitting at
the Superior Court at the time, describes as follows some indicators of
testamentary capacity:

[24]

Indicators of
testamentary capacity.
In a most useful
paper published in 2011, Professor Christine Morin explains that a number of
propositions regarding the indicators of testamentary capacity can be gleaned
from the cases.

[25]

Naturally, the testator’s
health and cognitive status are highly relevant facts in cases such as the
present one.
However, the fact that a testator is
of an advanced age is usually not considered, in itself, to be a particularly
probative indicator of testamentary incapacity.
Furthermore, courts
have underscored that a testator’s ability to carry out a normal conversation
and think rationally tends not to be determinative of testamentary capacity.

As the Supreme Court pointed out in a 1944 case which is still cited on this
point, “there is no doubt whatever that we may have testamentary incapacity
accompanied by a deceptive ability to answer questions of ordinary and usual
matters”.

[26]

Other relevant indicators
of testamentary capacity include the testator’s behaviour at the time the will
was made, as well as the extent to which that behaviour appears consistent with
how he or she usually behaved in certain circumstances
.

[27]

The terms of the will can
also provide useful clues
. Although courts cannot
question the wisdom or fairness of a testator’s choices in respect of the
distribution of their assets, testamentary provisions that seem
irrational, incoherent or otherwise unexplainable may, in appropriate
circumstances, constitute circumstantial evidence of incapacity.

[28]

Courts also tend to look closely to the circumstances surrounding
the making of the will.
Suspicious circumstances
may include the haste with which the will was made, the non-involvement of
legal professionals from whom the testator usually seeks advice, as well as the
lack of satisfactory explanations as to why a previous will was
changed. In a recent decision in which a will was found invalid on grounds
of incapacity, Justice Danielle Turcotte found relevant the fact that, when the
will was made, no one asked the testator objective and non-leading questions to
verify her intentions.

(References omitted; emphasis added)

[
29
]

Confusion created by the circumstances
surrounding the drafting of the will may impact on the testator’s capacity to
give consent.
[13]

[
30
]

The Court shall refrain from judging the choices
or values of the testator or appreciate the equity of his decisions.
[14]

[
31
]

The testator’s choices shall not be examined in
comparison to the choices of a reasonable person in the abstract, but in light
of his own values and personal characteristics. The objective is to assess whether
the testamentary provisions are coherent when examined in function of the
testator.
[15]

The Court should also be aware that witnesses could be tempted to give their
views on the testators’ consent in light of their own appreciation of what was
reasonable in the circumstances.
[16]

[
32
]

Finally, as for any contract, the testator must
not only be apt to express his consent, but his consent must be free and
enlightened.
[17]

If the testator’s consent is vitiated by error, fear or undue influence, his
testamentary dispositions are not the expression of his own will.
[18]

[
33
]

The situation where the testator does not have
capacity to formulate consent as regards dispositions of his will is distinct
from the situation where the testator has capacity to consent but his consent
is vitiated by error, fear or undue influence.

1.2

Discussion
as to Facts and Circumstances

[
34
]

The particular circumstances of this case raise
a definite concern regarding Mr. Moore's capacity to
understand and reasonably appreciate the meaning and effects of his testamentary
dispositions when he signed the Will on February 12,
2014, because:

-

His mental condition had declined in recent
years; his short-term memory was impaired and he was confused at times. His
medical record reports a mild cognitive impairment (
“MCI”
);

-

The Will significantly alters the way his estate
is divided among his children, in comparison with the provisions of his
previous manuscript will and compared with the testamentary dispositions
discussed on several occasions with his advisors up to a year prior. The Will
places Lianne at a disadvantage, whereas Mr. Moore's intention was always to
divide his estate equally between his children;

-

The Will was signed in haste, while Mr. Moore
had been reluctant to sign a new will for years;

-

The Will was signed in a climate of urgency and
fear conveyed upon Mr. Moore principally by John and suscitated by Lianne's
apprehended marriage to a person who had a criminal record;

-

The sense of urgency to act was unwarranted;

-

John initiated the process to schedule a meeting
with lawyer Robert Raich to sign the Will before Mr. Moore manifested any
intent of doing the Will;

-

John and others advised Mr. Moore on conditions
of the Will;

-

There was no probing of Mr. Moore's capacity to
appreciate the impacts of his new testamentary provisions on Lianne.

[
35
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court finds
that the preponderance of evidence establishes that Mr. Moore did not have the
capacity to form a valid consent under the above circumstances.

1.2.1

The Objections Raised Regarding the Evidence

1.2.1.1

Exhibit JL-37: Letter from Dr. Kinnear dated
February 11, 2016

[
36
]

John and Mtre Liber ask to introduce into
evidence a letter from Dr. Douglas G. Kinnear, addressed to John, in which he
replies to a request from the Executors of the Estate. Dr. Kinnear provides the
reader with his comments on the deceased’s mental status on or about the period
of January/ February 2014.

[
37
]

Dr. Kinnear acted as the team doctor for the
Montreal Canadians and Mr. Moore came under his care in 1962. He later on
became his family doctor. He saw him in his office as well as socially.

[
38
]

Dr. Kinnear passed away before the trial and was
not examined out of court.

[
39
]

John and Mtre Liber invoke the application of article
2870 C.C.Q. This provision reads as follows:

2870.
A statement made by a person who does not appear as a witness,
concerning facts to which he could have legally testified, is admissible as
testimony on application and after notice is given to the adverse party,
provided the court authorizes it.

The court shall, however, ascertain
that it is impossible for the declarant to appear as a witness, or that it is
unreasonable to require him to do so, and that the reliability of the statement
is sufficiently guaranteed by the circumstances in which it is made.

Reliability is presumed to be
sufficiently guaranteed with respect in particular to documents drawn up in the
ordinary course of business of an enterprise, to documents entered in a
register required by law to be kept, and spontaneous statements that are contemporaneous
to the occurrence of the facts.

[
40
]

Article 2870 C.C.Q. introduces an exception to
the standard rule that witnesses are called to testify before the courts, after
having solemnly declared that they will say the whole truth. This exception edicted
by article 2870 C.C.Q. applies under the specific conditions that the
appearance of the declarant is impossible or unreasonable, that the reliability
of the statement is sufficiently guaranteed by the circumstances in which it is
made and that the statement concerns facts to which the declarant could have
legally testified
[19]
.

[
41
]

The analysis conducted by the Court must
consider the fact that the credibility of the author of the document will not
be appreciated directly and will not be subjected to a cross-examination.
[20]

[
42
]

Article 2870 C.C.Q. cannot serve to introduce
into evidence an opinion. As the Court of Appeal explains in
Dubé
c.
Cliché
,
[21]
this provision does not have
for object to allow to introduce into evidence the report of an expert, who, in
principle, is not considered as a witness of facts:

30
En l'espèce, il n'est pas nécessaire de
décider si les deux premières conditions sont remplies puisque la troisième
n'est pas satisfaite. En effet, les rapports du Vérificateur ne se limitent pas
à l'énumération de «
faits
» au sujet desquels il aurait pu «
légalement
»
témoigner. Certes, dans une infime portion, les rapports énoncent de tels
faits, mais ils contiennent également, dans une portion appréciable, des
éléments de ouï-dire, des conclusions, des recommandations, des interprétations
de la réglementation, des opinions, etc. qui ne peuvent être introduits en
preuve par la déclaration dont traite
l'
article
2870

C.c.Q.
Cette
disposition n'a pas pour objectif de permettre le dépôt en preuve d'un rapport
d'expert ni celui d'un enquêteur, parce que, en principe, ceux-ci ne peuvent
être considérés comme des témoins de «
faits
».

[
43
]

John and Mtre Liber raise that Dr. Kinnear could
have validly testified at trial regarding his medical observations of his
patient’s cognitive condition.

[
44
]

Lianne objects to the filing of Dr. Kinnear’s
letter on the basis that it formulates an opinion. Subsidiarily, she invokes
that only a redacted version of the letter including only factual background can
be produced.

[
45
]

The circumstances in which Dr. Kinnear’s letter
was addressed and its contents leave no doubt as regards its nature and purpose.
He states that he was asked to comment on the mental status of the deceased on
or about January / February 2014. He gives background pertinent to
his
opinion to follow
. He states that he is
given to understand
that
at that time, Mr. Moore prepared his final will and last testament. He declares
that he
can state with confidence
that Mr. Moore was
fully compos
mentis
at the time. He then adds that
his thinking was clear;
he was

oriented, his judgment was sharp, his insight good and his behaviour at all
times responsible.

[
46
]

To the Court, this statement is clearly of the
nature of an opinion written by a medical professional having known the
deceased both professionally and socially and who shares his views on the
deceased’s capacity at the time of his Will. The letter is concise and does not
relate many of the facts on which it rests, apart from the description that Mr.
Moore was still driving his car, going daily to his office and was active in
many social events in the community. We are not aware to which extent Dr. Kinnear
had personal knowledge of these facts in particular, apart from his statement
that he enjoyed numerous interactions with him, the timing of which is not declared.
The probative value of that part of Dr. Kinnear’s statement is uncertain.

[
47
]

The Court finds that the letter in itself constitutes
an opinion and the excerpts of Dr. Kinnear’s statements which relate his views,
comments or judgment on Mr. Moore’s mental status cannot be introduced by
virtue of
article 2870
C.C.Q.

[
48
]

The Court will allow into evidence the first
part of the letter and exclude the third paragraph, from “
I can state
(…)”
until “(…)
responsible
”
,
being understood that the probative
value of the contents allowed is subject to appreciation.

[
49
]

At this stage of the admissibility of the
evidence, the Court does not need to be convinced of the veracity of the
contents of the statement. Its probative value will be appreciated in light of
the complete evidence.
[22]

1.2.1.2

Dr. Kinnear’s Interview with the Defendant’s Expert
on September 29, 2017

[
50
]

Dr. Kinnear was interviewed by Dr. Frank, the
expert mandated by John and Mtre Liber, for the purpose of conducting his
expertise. John and Mtre Liber wish to file into evidence Dr. Frank’s typing of
this interview, again based on
article 2870
C.C.Q.

[
51
]

1.2.2.1

The Common Views of the Experts

[
74
]

The Court finds that the experts both agree on
the following.

[
75
]

The assessment of testamentary capacity
necessitates the verification of the presence of basic conditions at the time
the Will was signed.

[
76
]

The testator must understand what a last will
and testament is, he must know who are his heirs, what his assets are. The testator
must be able to appreciate what impact his testamentary decisions may have on
his surviving heirs. The testator must have the requisite cognitive abilities
such as full consciousness, adequate executive thinking functions, the ability
to reason, and to communicate adequately with the notary or lawyer.

[
77
]

Mr. Moore demonstrated, in the last several
years of his life, a certain degree of cognitive impairment, characterized as
mild cognitive impairment, as diagnosed by his neurologist Dr. Eric Ehrensperger.
[29]
His short-term memory was
impaired and the results of a MoCA
[30]

test indicate that certain of his cognitive functions were affected. Mr. Moore
showed a lack of insight relating to his condition and denied his memory lapses
to his neurologist.
[31]

His condition resulted in the prevailing of a certain vulnerability.

[
78
]

A diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment implies
that the cognitive deficits do not prevent the pursuance of some independent
daily activities, although some efforts and strategies on the person's part may
be required to compensate for whatever cognitive difficulties exist.

[
79
]

A medical or psychiatric diagnosis does not, on
its own,  inform one about a given individual's capacity to create a last will.

[
80
]

The assessment of capacity requires the analysis
of the interaction between the complexity of the task and the underlying mental
capacities.

[
81
]

The testimony of persons surrounding the
testator at the relevant time and their description of his general demeanour
can assist the Court in this determination.

[
82
]

The experts expressed different opinions on
other aspects of the issue of capacity. Here is a summary of the evidence retained
by the Court from both experts.

John came back with his suggestion in this new context where fear of
Bowen was induced upon Mr. Moore.

[
206
]

Furthermore, Mtre Liber testifies that on that day, when asked who
would manage the business, Mr. Moore first responded that both children could
do so. Mtre Liber then suggested to Mr. Moore that he chooses only one of the
two in case they have diverging opinions. It is then, according to Mtre Liber,
that Mr. Moore decided that it would be John who would run the business.

[
207
]

Clearly, not only Mr. Moore did not initiate the process to do the
Will, but he was influenced by suggestions from others as regards important
testamentary dispositions.

[
208
]

This influence came in the context of the sense of urgency and fear
described earlier and was exerted on a testator who showed vulnerability.

[
209
]

It is under those circumstances that Mr. Moore came to sign a Will
which alters significantly what he had always contemplated in the past
regarding his estate and the future of his children.

1.2.8

The Explanations Advanced Behind the Changes Established
in the Will

[
210
]

Nothing documents Mr. Moore’s reasoning behind the changes which are
introduced in the Will.

[
211
]

The drastic changes regarding the treatment reserved to Lianne in
the Will can only be explained by the sense of urgency and fear of the
consequences of a wedding between Lianne and Bowen, induced upon Mr. Moore,
conjugated with his incapacity of appreciating the consequences of those new
provisions upon Lianne.

[
212
]

The Court is not satisfied that the Lianne Trust was put into place
to protect Lianne from herself because she was spendthrift or irresponsible.

[
213
]

Indeed, her lifestyle had been well known to Mr. Moore and had never
been raised during prior discussions with his lawyers concerning the drafting
of his will.

[
214
]

Furthermore, the testimony of Vincent convinces that Mr. Moore was
not any less in disagreement and displeased by the luxurious spending habits of
his son.

[
215
]

It is true that the evidence demonstrates that Mr. Moore was
apparently annoyed that the work carried out by Bowen to renovate Lianne’s
house did not justify the importance of his invoicing. However, the work was
paid for under his approval. According to John, Bowen was even present at the Easter
family brunch in April 2014.

[
216
]

Even if we accept that Mr. Moore had a genuine concern to protect
Lianne from her spendthrift behaviour, an incomprehensible disconnect manifests
between the provisions of the Will and Mr. Moore’s intent of treating his
children equally.

[
217
]

There is also an unexplainable disconnect with regards to the amount
of the allowance of $ 5,000 stipulated in the Will, and even more if we
consider the minimal amount of $ 2,000 which Mr. Moore would have
first suggested, if we compare those amounts to the financial support which Mr.
Moore always afforded to Lianne during his lifetime.

[
218
]

Given Mr. Moore’s feelings towards his daughter and his intent of
being fair towards her and advantage his children equally upon his death, the
change of treatment expressed in the Will can only be explained by an
incapacity on his part of understanding the effect of those important changes
on Lianne.

[
219
]

The Court finds that Mr. Moore, given his vulnerability, the sense
of urgency and the sense of a need for protection against Bowen, was probably confused
and led to understand that he still provided for an equal apportionment of his
estate between his children. Indeed, the wording of the Will invites to such incorrect
understanding when it stipulates that the Trustees shall “
divide the capital
of the Trust Property as it then exists into equal shares for each child of
mine
…”.

[
220
]

As regards the new provision concerning the management of the
business entrusted to John, one could reasonably consider that it was reasonable
for Mr. Moore to designate his son, given his actual involvement in the
operations, administration and finance.

[
221
]

However, such had not been the view of Mr. Moore, except for a brief
period in 2011, while he was not on his own but accompanied by Vincent, Mr. Zingboim
and Mtre Liber.

[
222
]

Apart from that episode, Mr. Moore never expressed the intent that
only John would manage the business after his passing.

[
223
]

And this only time that he thought of providing for such attribution,
he took the care of requiring a protection for his daughter’s long life
employment.

[
224
]

This drastic change of provision was made in haste. On the same
morning, Mr. Moore’s first answer was that both children could run the
business. John feared to be managing the business with Lianne and Bowen and
this is the reason why the Will was drafted accordingly.

[
225
]

Such a drastic change was based on an induced unwarranted sense of
urgency, and without taking the time to provide for protections for Lianne.

[
226
]

Perhaps this designation appeared to be reasonable to the lawyers,
but it did not corresponded to Mr. Moore’s desire until things turned on a span
of a few minutes on that day.

1.2.9

The Demeanour of Mr. Moore on the Day of his
Will and the Absence of Probing

[
227
]

Dr. Shulman well explains that circumstances like these require from
the testator a higher level of intellectual faculties to enable him to think
independently, understand and appreciate the effects of his testamentary
dispositions on his heirs, and resist to influence from others.

[
228
]

The evidence demonstrates that the discussions surrounding the
drafting of the Will and the subsequent reading and signing were performed in a
context where the professionals advance that they did not doubt Mr. Moore’s
capacity. They hence did not probe or verify his understanding of the changes
brought to the provisions of the draft will and their effects upon Lianne.

[
229
]

The following observations explain why the Court comes to the
conclusion that there was no probing of the capacity of Mr. Moore to understand
those important changes and to appreciate their impact on Lianne.

[
230
]

As confirmed by Mtre Raich, this was the first time that he
discussed a testamentary trust with Mr. Moore. This was the first time that a
limited instalment for Lianne was raised.This was the first time that it was
discussed enclosing in the Will that John would run the business.

[
231
]

The evidence does not show that measures were taken to verify the
extent of Mr. Moore’s understanding of the effects of those provisions of
the Will.

[
232
]

The professionals explain that they perceived no reason to doubt of
Mr. Moore’s capacity of understanding the provisions which were discussed.

[
233
]

Mtre Raich describes that Mr. Moore appeared consistent with the man
he had known for 30 years. He was taciturn and quiet as always, but upset
because of the upcoming wedding. He had particular demands in view of this
upcoming marriage and Lianne’s profligate ways. He found a solution to his concerns.
To him, Mr. Moore listened and understood his advice of setting up a trust.

[
234
]

Mtre Liber declares that Mr. Moore was expressive and clear as to
what he wanted. This contradicts the ambivalence and change of his mind
regarding the designation of who would run the business.

[
235
]

The evidence does not show that discussions were held with Mr. Moore
to explain the extent to which the arrangements put in place for Lianne
deviated from her current advantages and would ultimately result in the estate
not being divided equally.

[
236
]

Discussions were not held to ensure that Mr. Moore understood that
Lianne would not receive the entire capital of her share of the estate and that
John’s children would ultimately benefit from the capital of the trust upon her
death. Mr. Moore had particularly mentioned that he did not wish to advantage
his grandchildren in the Will, leaving to John the responsibility of taking
care of his own children. Vincent explains that he himself did not understand
that Lianne would not be getting her share of the capital of the estate. Mtre Liber
also confirms that it was not specifically discussed that Lianne would not get
her share of the capital.

[
237
]

The evidence does not show that explanations were given regarding
the conflictual situation of John acting both as a father to his children, eventual
beneficiaries of the Lianne Trust, and as Trustee of the Lianne Trust, having
the discretion of voting for or against an encroachment.

[
238
]

The evidence does not show that Mr. Moore was asked whether
particular protections should be afforded to Lianne as regards her employment, despite
the fact that specific protection had been discussed with Mtre Liber in 2011.

[
239
]

There was also no probing at the time of the reading of the Will.

[
240
]

Mtre Raich was no longer present when the Will was read and signed.

[
241
]

It is Mtre Lydinia who would have read the Will to Mr. Moore. She
describes having done so word by word, pointing out the modifications. He
followed and nodded. The exercice lasted 30 minutes. He did not raise the fact
that there is an error in the Will as regards the bequest to his nephew’s
children, where they are referred to as being his grandchildren. He was so
grateful to her and the notary.

[
242
]

Surprisingly, Mtre Liber has a different recollection of the reading.
He remembers that the reading of the Will was performed by the notary line by
line. He describes that Mr. Moore listened and did not ask questions.

[
243
]

The notary does not recall much of this mandate. He recalls nothing
unusual or eventful regarding the testator’s general demeanour. He explains
that in general for this type of mandate, he asks the testator if he is
familiar with the will, if it expresses his wishes and if he understands. He
asks if he waives reading and then proceeds with the signing. He assumes that
the lawyers have gone over the will with the testator.

[
244
]

The Court concludes that there were no discussions on that day which
would have enabled to confirm that Mr. Moore understood and appreciated the
effects of the provisions of the Will on Lianne.

1.2.10

After the Will

[
245
]

On the day of the signature of the Will, Mr. Moore brought the
necessary documentation to Lianne to sign for the issuance of LEECO shares to
his name and to obtain her resignation as a director. The documents in question
were remitted to Mr. Moore by Mtre Lydinia before they left the lawyers’
office.

[
246
]

Two weeks after signing the Will, Mr. Moore became confused when
Lianne asked him to write her a check to cover for her expenses. Questions
arise when it comes to finding an explanation to this confusion. Was it linked
to his medical condition? Was it confusing for Mr. Moore to continue to pay for
important expenses while he had stipulated for a limited allowance two weeks
prior? Had he realized that the allowance provision was not an immediate
protective measure? That it would prevail after his death? The evidence shows
that Mr. Moore was then directed by Vincent to issue payment to Lianne, as
always. Vincent explains:
[77]

“(…) I called Mr. Moore. He seemed
lost, he didn’t know. He said, "
What’s this she wants me to sign? What
is this
"; you know? So, I said, "
Look, Mr. Moore, it’s —
"Mr. Dickie, it’s her regular — it’s her expense cheque
." I said,
"
You’ve signed them before. You can sign this one
." So, he
said, "
Okay
."

[
247
]

What is also perplexing is that it is with John and Vincent that
Mtre Raich communicated later in March 2014 regarding tax planning
[78]
. If Mr. Moore was as sharp as
he had been 30 years prior and readily capable of discussing issues of this
sort, why isn’t he the one with whom Mtre Raich would address the issues
regarding tax planning?

[
248
]

Another aspect of the evidence is puzzling.

[
249
]

The Will was addressed to the attention of Mr. Moore by the notary.
The accompanying letter is addressed to Mr. Moore’s home address in the Town of
Mount Royal where he no longer resided at the time. No envelope is available to
ascertain that the Will was sent by mail.

[
250
]

According to John, the Will was found after the trial in Mr. Moore’s
safe at Moore Equipment. John asserts that he never opened the safe until then.
It is only when the Court asked whether the evidence indicated if Mr. Moore had
received the Will that John apparently thought of opening the safe, close to
ten years after his father’s death.

[
251
]

This testimony lacks probative value. John acts as liquidator and
the Court finds surprising that the safe, which at some point contained funds
in cash,  would never have been opened by him. The plaintiff’s lawyers
underline rightfully that John wrote to Mtre Raich in July 2015 to obtain a
digital copy of the Will and mandate, suggesting that he was aware of a paper
version.

[
252
]

After hearing the complete evidence, the Court finds unconceivable
that John would never have verified whether his father received a copy of the
Will before he passed away.

[
253
]

This questionable evidence brings to set aside John’s suggestion
that Mr. Moore would have received the Will and carefully placed it inside his
safe.

[
254
]

Finally, the Court finds troubling that no one did discuss with Mr.
Moore afterwards the fact that he had signed the Will urgently in view of the
upcoming wedding of Lianne and that finally, this wedding was not taking place.

1.3

Conclusion

[
255
]

The Court finds that Mr. Moore could not reasonably have consented
to change his testamentary provisions to an extent that it would create an
inequitable sharing of his estate between his children. He had always wanted to
share his estate equally between his two children and this intent is still specifically
expressed in the Will.

[
256
]

The same conclusion prevails as regards the provision which excludes
Lianne from managing the companies, which was decided on the spot, after Mr.
Moore first advanced that both his children could manage the business.

[
257
]

The only reasonable explanation as to why Mr. Moore seemed to express
his consent to the stipulation of testamentary provisions with detrimental effects
on Lianne is that he was not able to understand their
meaning nor measure their effects on his daughter.

[
258
]

Mr. Moore was vulnerable and his cognitive functions were impaired.
He needed assistance for certain tasks. He certainly would have necessitated
more explanations to understand the impacts of the Lianne Trust on Lianne and
clarifications to enhance that contrary to what was simply put forward, the
concrete effect of his Will would be that in the end, his estate would not be
shared equally.

[
259
]

He certainly also necessitated explanations as to what a change
regarding the exclusive management of the business by John entailed and to be
reminded of his past concerns to ensure Lianne’s involvement in the business
and her long-life employment.
[79]

[
260
]

Finally, the clauses in the Will stipulating the rights and
obligations of the Trustees as regards the voting rights on the shares of the
Moore Companies and on the division of the Estate and Trust Property have
necessary consequences on Lianne since she was excluded from that role. That
change necessitated explanations for Mr. Moore to be able to appreciate the
consequences for his daughter.

[
261
]

The evidence is that those explanations were not given.

[
262
]

The evidence is rather that the Will was signed in haste, at the
initiative of John and in a climate of fear and urgency, with many
participating in the discussion and Mr. Moore finally concurring with the
advice. Mr. Moore signed the Will understanding that the provisions were
necessary to protect the business from Bowen, but without understanding their
effects on Lianne. His misunderstanding was even more confused if he was led to
believe that the measures protected Lianne and were to her advantage.

[
263
]

No probing was performed on February 12, 2014, to verify Mr. Moore’s
specific understanding of the effects of the dispositions of the Will on Lianne
which could bring the Court to set aside this conclusion.

2.

The issue of undue influence

2.1

Legal
Principles

[
264
]

As the Court of Appeal recently reiterates in
Thivierge

c.
Thivierge
,
[80]

it is not illegitimate or illicit to attempt to influence someone regarding
the drafting of his will. The validity of a will may, however, be contested if
the influence is deemed to be undue.

[
265
]

Undue influence is assimilated to fraud and manifests in the
presence of lies, calumny, deceptions, stratagem or intentional false
statements which bring the testator to make decisions which he would not have made
otherwise:

[15]      Il n’y a rien
d’illégitime ou d’illicite à tenter d’influencer une personne dans la rédaction
de son testament. Toutefois, sa validité peut être contestée lorsqu'il est
établi que le testateur a été soumis à une pression indue. De la même manière,
la pression indue – ou captation – peut être invoquée pour annuler un acte de
donation. La captation, qui s’assimile à de la fraude, se manifeste par des
mensonges, des calomnies, des tromperies, des ruses ou de fausses déclarations
délibérées qui amènent le testateur ou le donateur à prendre des décisions
qu'il n'aurait pas prises autrement.

(References omitted)

[
266
]

As the Court of Appeal explains in
Brusenbauch

c.
Young
,
[81]

the burden of establishing undue influence (captation) rests on the plaintiff.
This burden may be discharged by direct or circumstantial evidence of facts
amounting to serious, precise and concordant presumptions:
[82]

[17]
The party alleging undue influence will discharge that burden by
direct or, more often (undue influence generally being a secret or covert
affair), circumstantial evidence, meaning evidence of facts – improper schemes,
disgraceful devices, lies, slander, deceit and trickery, or deliberate misrepresentations
– that constitute precise and concordant presumptions (art. 2849
C.C.Q.
)
and support such a finding.

(Reference omitted)

[
267
]

The applicable standard of proof remains proof on a balance of
probabilities and the question to be determined remains whether the impugned
will was more likely than not the result of undue influence.
[83]

2.2

Discussion

[
268
]

There exist two main reasons why the Court concludes that the
principles of undue influence do not apply to the present matter.

[
269
]

First, the Court concludes that Mr. Moore did not have the required
capacity to consent and appreciate the provisions of the Will and their effects
on Lianne. One cannot conclude that Mr. Moore’s consent was vitiated if he did
not have capacity from the beginning.

[
270
]

Second, although it appears sufficiently probable that John managed
to bring his father to sign the Will providing for provisions corresponding to
his views and that he probably benefited from the timing of Lianne’s announced wedding
to achieve his desire, the Court does not believe that his behaviour amounted
to fraud.

[
271
]

Indeed, John did everything in the open, with the apparent support
of Vincent, Mtre Liber and Mtre Raich.

[
272
]

In all appearance, the protagonists behind the Will were of the view
that a paternalistic approach towards Lianne constituted a most reasonable
business decision which ensured modalities meant to protect half of the Trust
Property.

[
273
]

Designating John to run the business upon his father’s death also
probably appeared logical not only to John, who felt that he more than deserved
the title, but also to Vincent and the lawyers, who were already used to dealing
with him.

[
274
]

The Court is convinced that the influence exerted upon Mr. Moore in
the circumstances described above brought him to sign the Will with conditions
which he would not have chosen otherwise.

[
275
]

However, the Court is not convinced that John’s behaviour amounted
to undue influence within the meaning developed by the jurisprudence for this
notion and which is assimilated to fraud.

2.3

Conclusion

[
276
]

Although Mr. Moore was influenced by John and others to execute the
Will and stipulate provisions detrimental to Lianne, the nullity of the Will
results from the testator’s incapacity and not from undue influence.

3.

The Issue of Foreclosure to Claim the Nullity of
the Will

[
277
]

Defendants plead that Lianne is legally foreclosed and has renounced
to any legal right she may ever have had to set aside the Will, whether for
reasons related to legal capacity or otherwise.

3.1

Legal
Principles

[
278
]

The defendants invoke that pursuant to
article 773

C.c.Q.
, no person
having acknowledged a will may thereafter contest its validity:

773
. No
person having acknowledged a will may thereafter contest its validity, although
he may apply to have the will probated.

In the case of contestation of a
will which has been probated, the burden is on the person availing himself of
the will to prove its origin and regularity.

[
279
]

It appears uncertain to the Court that such provision would apply to
a notarized will.

[
280
]

Indeed, the provision is stipulated under chapter VI of the
Civil
Code

of Quebec
entitled
Proof and Probate of Wills
, which do
not apply to a notarized will. Proof of a notarized will is covered by articles
regarding the means of proof of authentic acts under articles 2813 and
following.

[
281
]

Articles 1420 and 1423 C.C.Q. could, however, apply to the situation
where a will affected by relative nullity is later confirmed:

1420.
The relative nullity of a contract may be invoked only by the
person in whose interest it is established or by the other contracting party,
provided he is acting in good faith and suffers serious injury therefrom; it
may not be invoked by the court of its own motion.

A contract
that is relatively null may be confirmed.

[…]

1423.
The confirmation of a
contract results from the express or tacit will to renounce the invocation of
its nullity.

The will to confirm must be certain
and evident.

[
282
]

Confirmation under article 1423 or acknowledgement under
article 773

both require the prior knowledge of the existence of the cause of annulment of
the contract.

[
283
]

The renunciation to invoke the nullity must be clear and
unequivocal. The simple passage of time does not suffice to conclude to
renunciation
[84]
.

3.2

Discussion
as to Relevant Facts and Circumstances

[
284
]

As early as January 19, 2016, Lianne’s lawyer requested a report
from Dr. Mulder in connection with Mr. Moore’s state of health and mental
capacities.
[85]

He received a reply that Mr. Moore’s capacities were normal on February 2,
2016.
[86]

[
285
]

On February 3, 2016, Lianne’s attorneys addressed a first demand
letter to the defendants formulating the following reserve of rights:
[87]

“We have been provided with a copy
of your letter dated January 19, 2016 addressed specifically to our client and,
under reserve of any and all of her rights, recourses and remedies, and without
any acknowledgment as to the validity of the said Last Will and Testament, we
hereby wish to address certain aspects of your letter, (…)”.

[
286
]

Other correspondence exchanged on Lianne’s behalf also expressly
reserved her rights. For instance, on February 16, 2016, in a letter
acknowledging receipt of three payments of $ 5,000:
[88]

Please be advised that Ms. Moore
will negotiate the aforesaid cheque on account of her claims and under express
reserve of any and all of her rights, remedies and recourses; such negotiation
not to be construed as a renunciation and/or ratification of any kind.

[
287
]

Lianne also reserved her rights to demand the annulment of the Will
in her
Originating demand
in April 2017
and
alleged at the time Mr. Moore’s impaired condition:
[89]

“
Reserve
unto the Plaintiff
Lianne
J. Moore
all of her rights, remedies and recourses, including those
relating to the validity of the
Last Will and Testament
of the
Late
Richard W. Moore
executed before Notary Mtre Abby Malkinson on
February
12, 2014
, and recorded under number
16488
of his minutes.”

[
288
]

Lianne sought orders to obtain communication of Mr. Moore’s medical
files
in order for Lianne to be in possession of all of the facts and
information required for the proper and full exercise of all of her rights and
recourses including those being already exercised hereunder
”.

[
289
]

The Court finds that Lianne clearly reserved her rights at all
relevant times and that there exists no renunciation on her part to claim for
the nullity of the Will.

3.3

Conclusion

[
290
]

Lianne is not forclosed from invoking the nullity of the Will.

4.

The Remedy

[
291
]

The Court asked the parties to submit further arguments regarding the
possibility of concluding to the partial nullity of the Will.

[
292
]

Indeed, the expert evidence convinces that the assessment of
capacity requires the analysis of the interaction between the complexity of the
task and the underlying mental capacities of the testator. The more complex a
testamentary disposition, the more concern regarding the capacity to understand
its effects, depending on the scheme of circumstances.

[
293
]

The corollary to this would be that capacity to give valid consent
to simple testamentary dispositions is less susceptible of raising a concern.

[
294
]

The evidence establishes that the specific
bequests to family members and employees provided by articles 5 and 6 of the
Will had been the object of discussion since 2011
[90]
and have remained unchanged
in the Will. The dispositions are straightforward and simply enunciate amounts
destined to family members and close employees.The understanding of the effect
of those bequests does not appear to reveal any complexity nor particular
difficulty.

[
295
]

Those bequests are not the object of any
contestation on the part of the parties. Lianne does not raise concern
regarding those bequests and has even confirmed that she would not claim that
they be reimbursed should the Will be declared invalid.

[
296
]

For the reasons which follow, the Court finds
that those specific bequests should be maintained.

4.1

Legal
Principles

[
297
]

The doctrine suggests that complete nullity should, in principle, be
envisaged as the normal course of action in the event of incapacity, while
partial nullity could be sanctioned in the presence of a defect of consent.

[
298
]

The authors Beaulne and Morin are of this opinion and they address
the question as follows:
[91]

703.
—
Étendue
de la nullité.
— Qu’il y ait absence de volonté ou vice de
volonté, la sanction est la nullité. Encore faut-il en
déterminer l’étendue. Au cas d’insanité d’esprit, la sanction
est normalement une nullité globale, puisque, par hypothèse, le
testateur ne savait pas ce qu’il faisait. Lorsque c’est un vice de consentement
qui est invoqué, la nullité pourra n’être que partielle. Il
se peut en effet qu’un legs ait été consenti par erreur, ou sous l’empire
de la crainte, alors que les autres l’ont été librement et en toute
connaissance de cause.

[
299
]

This opinion is based on the premise that in case of incapacity, the
testator does not, normally, have the required capacity as regards the will as
a whole. This hypothesis is based on a factual assumption.

[
300
]

The Court acknowledged the potential nullity of a particular
testamentary disposition as the remedy for undue influence in
Gardiner
(Estate of)
c.
Young
:
[92]

[71] Undue influence or “captation”
can give rise to the nullity of a particular testamentary disposition or to the
entire testament itself when it is the result of and is accompanied by fraud of
such nature that, but for its presence, the testator would not otherwise have
made the bequests subject to challenge.

[
301
]

The Court of Appeal in
Khan
c.
Katiya
,
[93]

also confirms that article 1438 C.C.Q. sets out a rule for contracts which is
transposable to wills. This provision reads as follows:

1438
.   A clause which is null does not render the
contract invalid in other respects, unless it is apparent that the contract may
be considered only as an indivisible whole.

The same applies to a
clause that is without effect or that is deemed unwritten.

[
302
]

The Court is unaware of examples of partial
nullity for incapacity in the case law.

[
303
]

In principle, if the Will is null as a whole, it
is deemed never
to have existed
, as provided by article 1422 C.C.Q.

4.2

Discussion

[
304
]

The Court finds that Mr. Moore
probably had the capacity to understand
the extent and significance of the provisions of the Will which concerned the
specific bequests to employees and family members.

[
305
]

Those
provisions had been decided prior to February 12, 2014. They were decided in
the absence of influence from others, outside the climate of urgency and fear of
Bowen and not in reaction to an induced need for protection. Those provisions
are completely distinct and separate from the sections of the Will which
concern John and Lianne and are totally remote from the contextual analysis
which brought the Court to conclude to Mr. Moore’s incapacity as regards those
sections.

[
306
]

The Court believes that it is in the interest of justice that those
specific bequests remain.

[
307
]

This conclusion conforms to the principles of law and it appears
that it rightly and judicially adapts to the particular circumstances of this
matter.

[
308
]

Aside from those specific bequests, the provisions of the Will
appear to be intrinsically related and to form part of an indivisible whole. The
Court concludes that the nullity of the Will should be pronounced, except for
the specific bequests.
